summary: In this streamlined second edition of Martin Wallace's classic, players build up a personal tableau of London cards representing buildings and districts, then periodically 'run the city' to trigger all their cards' income and poverty effects at once. The tension comes from balancing borrowed money and expansion against the poverty you generate, since loans must be repaid before the game ends and unchecked poverty actively hurts you.
praised: elegant tension between expansion and poverty management
streamlined rules compared to the dense original edition
strong sense of building a personal city identity
criticised: some take-that poverty-dumping cards can feel mean
limited direct interaction beyond drafting and poverty effects
can feel like solitaire engine-building between the shared draft moments
less thematic depth than some city-building peers

interaction.kind: occasional take-that cards plus a relative-poverty comparison at scoring
interaction.detail: Most turns involve building an individual card tableau and running your own city, so direct conflict is intermittent rather than constant. But some cards actively hinder opponents, and poverty is scored relative to what everyone else generates, so a portion of the shared state genuinely depends on others' choices rather than existing purely as personal progress.
interaction.said: generally seen as a fairly solitaire engine-builder despite its 'Take That' tag — reviewers describe it as 'you're mostly building your own tableau' with only occasional nasty cards, and note poverty is judged 'relative to the other players'

scoring.how_you_win: Players play cards to build up London and then 'run the city' to trigger their effects, balancing income against poverty; when the deck runs out, players total building points minus poverty (relative to others) and loan penalties, and the highest score wins.
